The Wild West? Mapping Crime and Socioeconomic Patterns Across Greater Sydney



A GIS Analysis of Crime Hotspots and Socioeconomic Factors

Whilst nothing is explicitly described, this project discusses, explores and names a wide range of criminal offences. Many of these offences (particually those classified under Violent Crime) are confronting and may be upsetting for some readers/viewers.

If you have experienced violence or sexual assault and need immediate or ongoing help, contact 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732) to talk to a counsellor from the national sexual assault and domestic violence hotline. For confidential support and information, contact Safe Steps’ 24/7 family violence response line on 1800 015 188.

If you have concerns about your safety or that of someone else, please contact the police in your state or territory, or call Triple Zero (000) for emergency help.

Crime does not occur uniformly across cities. Understanding where offences are concentrated, and how these patterns vary between communities, can help reveal important spatial differences in public safety (Rosser et al., 2017). Geographic Information Systems (GIS) provide tools to map these patterns, identify crime hotspots and investigate how crime rates vary across different areas.

How does the spatial distribution of crime (drug offences, violent crime and property offences) vary across NSW LGAs, and to what extent is crime rate associated with unemployment, income and high-school completion?

This project uses GIS to investigate the spatial distribution of recorded crime across selected Local Government Areas (LGAs) in Greater Sydney between 2015 and 2025. It identifies areas with higher concentrations of crime and explores whether crime rates are associated with socioeconomic characteristics, including unemployment, weekly household income and high-school completion.

The relationship between crime and socioeconomic conditions is important when examining differences in crime rates between urban areas. Weatherburn (1992) explores the relationship between economic adversity and crime, while Walker and Henderson (1991) discuss Australian crime trends and the importance of considering social and demographic factors when interpreting crime statistics. Together, these studies highlight the value of examining socioeconomic conditions alongside geographic crime patterns.

Sharma and Tailor (2023) further demonstrate the value of spatial analysis by investigating crime hotspots and urban characteristics in Surat, India. Their research compares spatial interpolation techniques and examines associations between crime, land use and road connectivity. Although their findings relate to a different urban context, the study highlights the importance of appropriate GIS methods when investigating spatial crime patterns. Further studies also demonstrate the value of GIS for identifying crime hotspots. Ansari and Kale (2014), in their study of Aurangabad City, used techniques including Kernel Density Estimation (KDE), Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) and Getis-Ord Gi* to identify concentrations of criminal activity. Similarly, Chainey, Tompson and Uhlig (2008) compared different crime hotspot mapping techniques, highlighting the importance of selecting appropriate methods for identifying spatial crime patterns. These studies provide a foundation for using GIS to investigate crime hotspots across Greater Sydney.

By combining crime data with socioeconomic information, this project aims to provide a clearer picture of how crime patterns vary geographically. Specifically, it explores the spatial distribution of crime and whether differences in crime rates correspond with variations in unemployment, household income and high-school completion. These relationships are examined as spatial associations rather than evidence that socioeconomic conditions directly cause crime.

GIS Project | Greater Sydney, New South Wales | 2015–2025

Three primary datasets were used to investigate the spatial and socioeconomic distribution of crime across selected Local Government Areas (LGAs) in Greater Sydney between January 2015 and December 2025. Crime incident data were obtained from the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR), LGA boundary data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS), and socioeconomic indicators from the 2021 Australian Census.

The datasets were cleaned, aggregated and integrated into a common spatial dataset to enable comparisons between crime patterns and socioeconomic characteristics. The following tables summarise the source data, file formats and their roles in the analysis.

The following sections provide further details of the data preparation, socioeconomic statistical analysis and spatial hotspot analysis. Expand each section to explore the methodology.

Data Collection and Preparation

Data sources

Three primary datasets were used in this study:

Dataset

Source

Purpose

Local Government Areas (2025)

Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS)

Provided polygon geometries and geographic identifiers for the 30 selected LGAs.

Recorded Criminal Incidents by Month by LGA

NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR)

Provided monthly recorded crime counts for 2015–2025.

2021 Census General Community Profile G01, G02 & G43

Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS)

Provided socioeconomic indicators for education, household income and labour force characteristics.

Crime classification

Recorded offences were grouped into three categories:

Drug offences: Possession, dealing, manufacturing and importing.

Violent crime: Abduction and kidnapping, assault, coercive control, homicide, intimidation, stalking and harassment, sexual offences, and robbery.

Property offences: Theft, arson and malicious damage to property.

Data preparation

Python was used to clean and integrate the datasets and perform the statsitical analysis. Streamlit was used to host the webmaps as an app and Jupyter Book to display present the porject.

The following libaries were used during this project:import geopandas as gpd
import rasterio
import xarray as xr
import leafmap
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plot
from scipy import stats

The workflow involved:

Selecting the 30 study-area LGAs using their geographic identifiers.

Filtering crime records to the selected LGAs and relevant offence categories.

Aggregating monthly crime records into annual counts for 2015–2025.

Calculating total recorded crime counts for each crime category across the study period.

Extracting the relevant socioeconomic indicators from the 2021 Census.

Joining crime and socioeconomic attributes to the LGA polygons using matching geographic identifiers.

Checking for missing values, inconsistent identifiers and invalid geometries.

The resulting spatial dataset provided a consistent geographic framework for mapping crime, calculating rates, identifying hotspots and examining socioeconomic associations.

Crime counts and rates

Total recorded incidents were calculated for each LGA and crime category across 2015–2025.

Crime rates were calculated using:\text{Crime rate} =
\frac{\text{Total recorded incidents (2015–2025)}}
{\text{Population denominator}}
\times 1000

This standardised measure expresses recorded incidents per 1,000 residents. The population denominator used in the analysis should be specified in the final methodology.

Socioeconomic Statistical Analysis

The socioeconomic analysis investigated associations between crime and four indicators: time, year 12 completion in the adult population, household income and unemployment.

Socioeconomic indicators

Education: Highest year of school completion, sourced from 2021 Census Table G01.

Household income: Median total weekly household income, sourced from 2021 Census Table G02.

Unemployment: Selected labour force statistics, sourced from 2021 Census Table G43.

Analytical approach

The socioeconomic indicators were compared with drug offences, violent crime and property offences to investigate potential relationships between socioeconomic conditions and crime. The socioeconomic variables represent conditions recorded at the 2021 Census, while crime data span 2015–2025. Pearson’s correlation coefficient is a value between -1 and 1 which quantifies how linear the relationship between 2 variables is. The signifigance threshold was a p value of 0.05. Pearson’s correlation coefficent represents assosiations between datasets, not nessesarily causation.

The analysis considered:

Relationships between socioeconomic characteristics and crime the whole of greater Sydney.

The change in crime rates over time in each individual LGA

Socioeconomic Correlation Analysis

Pearson’s correlation coeffcient was calculated for each crime type (rate per 1000 people for each LGA) and each socioeconomic variable (for each LGA) resulting in r and p values.

Time Correlation Analysis

The changes in crime rate over time (each year from 2015-2025) were plotted and then had a correlation coefficent calculated to see if there was a statistically signifigant relationship over time. CODE was used to perform a least squares analysis on the dataset to determine a linear (first order) line of best fit for the dataset. The slope value of this line of best fit was used to quantify the rate of change over time. LGAs which did not have a statistically signifigant change in crime rate over time were given a rate of change over time value of 0.

Spatial Hotspot Statistical Analysis

Getis–Ord Gi hotspot analysis*

Local Getis–Ord Gi* statistics were calculated to identify spatial clusters of high and low crime-rate values across neighbouring LGAs.

The analysis used:

Spatial weights: Queen contiguity, where LGAs are neighbours if their polygons share an edge or vertex.

Permutations: 199 permutations, selected because larger permutation counts caused computational problems.

Significance threshold: p < 0.05.

The results classified LGAs as hotspots, coldspots or not statistically significant, according to the calculated statistics and significance criteria.

Hotspots indicate areas where high values are spatially clustered relative to the spatial-randomness assumption. Coldspots indicate clusters of low values. Areas that do not meet the selected significance threshold are classified as not statistically significant.

Mapping and interpretation

The analysis produced thematic maps of crime counts, crime rates and hotspot classifications for drug offences, violent crime and property offences. These maps were used to compare the spatial patterns of each crime category and identify areas for further investigation.
